source.text: Ὅτε οὖν ἠρίστησαν λέγει τῷ Σίμωνι Πέτρῳ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Σίμων Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με πλέον τούτων;

records.literal_gloss: When therefore they had eaten breakfast, says to the Simon Peter the Jesus, "Simon of John, do you love me more than these?"

en.L: So when they had eaten breakfast, Jesus says to Simon Peter, "Simon [son] of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} more than these?"
en.B: After they had eaten breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} more than these?"
en.R: When they had finished eating, Jesus spoke to Simon Peter. "Simon, son of John," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} more than these others do?"

decisions.choice: love: the two verbs for love in 21:15-17 (ἀγαπάω, used by Jesus in his first two questions, and φιλέω, used by Peter in all three answers and by Jesus in the third question) are taken as having the same meaning here
alternatives: a distinction is meant: Jesus first asks for the fullest, self-giving love (ἀγαπάω), Peter can only answer with the love of a friend (φιλέω), and the third time Jesus comes down to Peter's own word
decisions.reason: John uses both verbs for the same love again and again: for the Father's love for the Son (3:35 ἀγαπᾷ; 5:20 φιλεῖ), for Jesus's love for Lazarus (11:5 ἠγάπα; 11:3 and 11:36 ἐφίλει), and for the disciple whom Jesus loved (13:23 ἠγάπα; 20:2 ἐφίλει). In this same passage he also varies the words for feeding and shepherding, for lambs and sheep, and for knowing (verses 15-17), with no change of sense. And verse 17 says Peter was grieved because Jesus asked a third time, not because he changed the verb. Still, the change of verb in the third question can be read as deliberate, and a footnote gives that view.

decisions.choice: more than these others love me
alternatives: more than you love these others
more than these things: the boat, the nets and the fishing (21:3)
decisions.reason: "These" can be masculine or neuter, and the comparison can be with what they do or with what Peter loves. Six other disciples are there (21:2), and Peter had once claimed a loyalty greater than theirs: he would lay down his life for Jesus (13:37; compare Mark 14:29, where he says he will stand firm even if all the others fall away). The question would then ask whether that claim still stands after his denials. But the words can also ask whether Peter loves Jesus more than he loves his friends, or more than the fishing he has just gone back to (21:3). In his reply Peter does not compare himself with anyone.

decisions.choice: son of John (SBLGNT), as in 1:42 and in verses 16 and 17
alternatives: son of Jonah, or Jonas (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts read John here, as at 1:42; many later ones read Jonah, as in Matthew 16:17 ("Bar-Jonah"). This John is Peter's father, not John the Baptist. Jesus uses Peter's full name, the name he had when Jesus first met him (1:42), not the name Peter that Jesus gave him. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the meal by the charcoal fire recalls the night of Peter's denials
decisions.reason: Jesus has just given the disciples breakfast of bread and fish by a charcoal fire (21:9-13). The word for a charcoal fire (ἀνθρακιά) is used in the New Testament only here (21:9) and at 18:18, where Peter stood warming himself and denied Jesus. Jesus now asks him three times about his love, as Peter had three times said he was not a disciple (18:17, 25-27).

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R); also in verses 15, 16, 17 and 19
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("he says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in English. This applies to every "says" in the passage (verses 15, 16, 17 and 19). "Said" in verse 17 is already a past tense in Greek.

decisions.choice: love, for both verbs, at every level
alternatives: love (for the first verb) and be fond of, or love as a friend (for the second)
decisions.reason: Both verbs are "love" throughout John (meaning decision m1), so they are "love" here too, at Literal as well. To give them different English words would decide the question the footnote leaves open, and would make Peter's answer sound weaker than it need be.

decisions.choice: more than these others do (R); Jesus spoke to Simon Peter ... he said
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "more than these", which leaves the comparison open. Readable says what meaning decision m2 finds most likely, so it is marked uncertain.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε.

records.literal_gloss: He says to him, "Yes, Lord, you know that I love you."

en.L: He says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Yes, Lord; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.B: Peter said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Yes, Lord, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.R: "Yes, Lord," Peter answered. "You know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: you know: Peter appeals to what Jesus himself knows
decisions.reason: "You" is stressed in Greek. After his denials Peter does not offer his own word as proof; he rests on Jesus's knowledge of him, which John has shown before (1:47-48; 2:24-25).

decisions.choice: Yes, I love you: Peter answers about his love but not about "more than these"
decisions.reason: Peter says yes to loving Jesus but makes no claim to love him more than the others. The man who once promised to lay down his life (13:37) now claims less. The verb he uses is the other verb for love (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: Lord: Peter's address to his risen master
decisions.reason: The disciples call Jesus "Lord" throughout John (6:68; 13:36-37), and in this chapter the disciple whom Jesus loved has just recognized him: "It is the Lord" (21:7).

decisions.choice: Peter said (B); Peter answered (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker so that the reader can follow who is speaking. Readable starts a new sentence at "You know", so that "You" takes a capital in any case.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ· Βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου.

records.literal_gloss: He says to him, "Feed the lambs of me."

decisions.choice: the lambs are the people who belong to Jesus; Peter is given a shepherd's work
decisions.reason: Jesus has called himself the good shepherd and his followers his sheep (10:11-16). He calls them "my" lambs: they remain his, and Peter is to care for them on his behalf. In the Scriptures God holds the shepherds of his people to account for feeding the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-16; Jeremiah 23:1-4), and Peter later gives the same charge to the elders of the churches (1 Peter 5:2).

decisions.choice: lambs: young sheep, standing here for the flock as a whole
alternatives: only the young or weak believers, as distinct from the sheep of verses 16-17
decisions.reason: The word (ἀρνίον) is used only here in John's Gospel. It is a different word from "the Lamb of God" in 1:29. Jesus goes on to say "sheep" in verses 16 and 17 with no sign of a change of flock; the variation is most likely one of style (see the decision on verse 17).

decisions.choice: Jesus said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus as the speaker, since the last speaker was Peter.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ πάλιν δεύτερον· Σίμων Ἰωάννου, ἀγαπᾷς με;

records.literal_gloss: He says to him again a second [time], "Simon of John, do you love me?"

en.L: He says to him again, a second [time], "Simon [son] of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.B: A second time he asked him, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.R: For the second time Jesus asked him, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: the second question drops "more than these"
decisions.reason: Jesus no longer asks Peter to compare himself with the others; he asks only whether Peter loves him. He uses the same verb as in the first question (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: again, a second time: the question is repeated on purpose
decisions.reason: John counts the questions ("a second time", "the third time" in verse 17), so that the reader sees three questions answering Peter's three denials (18:17, 25-27).

decisions.choice: A second time he asked him (B); For the second time Jesus asked him (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek verb is the ordinary "says" in the present tense (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15); Balanced and Readable say "asked" because it introduces a question, and put "a second time" first, which also covers "again". Readable names Jesus.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε.

records.literal_gloss: He says to him, "Yes, Lord, you know that I love you."

en.L: He says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Yes, Lord; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.B: Peter said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Yes, Lord, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.R: "Yes, Lord," Peter answered. "You know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: Peter repeats his first answer word for word
decisions.reason: The answer is the same as in verse 15, with the same verb for love and the same appeal to what Jesus knows (meaning decisions m1 and m2 at 21:15, second sentence).

decisions.choice: the same English as Peter's first answer, at each level
decisions.reason: Each level repeats its wording of verse 15 exactly, so that readers hear the repetition the Greek has.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ποίμαινε τὰ πρόβατά μου.

records.literal_gloss: He says to him, "Shepherd the sheep of me."

en.R: Jesus said to him, "Take care of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} sheep as a shepherd does."

decisions.choice: shepherd: do all of a shepherd's work, leading, guarding and providing for the flock
decisions.reason: The verb (ποιμαίνω) is wider than "feed" (βόσκω, verses 15 and 17): it covers the whole care of a shepherd for the flock. It shares a root with "shepherd" in 10:11-16, so Jesus gives Peter a share in his own work as the good shepherd. Peter uses the same verb when he charges the elders to shepherd God's flock (1 Peter 5:2).

decisions.choice: sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: little sheep: a diminutive form of the word (some early manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus)
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts read a diminutive form, "little sheep", here and in verse 17; others read the ordinary word for sheep, as the SBLGNT does. A diminutive like this was often used with no difference in meaning, so the sense is the same either way: the people who belong to Jesus (10:3-4, 14-16). A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Shepherd (L, B); Take care of ... as a shepherd does (R)
decisions.reason: "Shepherd" as a verb keeps the link with the good shepherd of 10:11-16 and keeps the two verbs of verses 15-17 apart (meaning decision m1). "Tend" is less common in everyday English. Readable spells out the picture in plain words.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ τὸ τρίτον· Σίμων Ἰωάννου, φιλεῖς με;

records.literal_gloss: He says to him the third [time], "Simon of John, do you love me?"

en.L: He says to him the third [time], "Simon [son] of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.B: A third time he asked him, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.R: For the third time Jesus asked him, "Simon, son of John, do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: love: Jesus now uses the verb Peter has been using, with the same meaning as before
alternatives: Jesus lowers his question to the lesser love Peter has claimed
decisions.reason: Here Jesus takes up Peter's own verb (φιλέω). If the two verbs mean the same (meaning decision m1 at 21:15, which has the footnote), the question is simply asked a third time; if a distinction is meant, Jesus now meets Peter where he is. Either way, verse 17 gives the third asking itself as the reason for Peter's grief.

decisions.choice: the third time: the last of three questions
decisions.reason: With the article the phrase means "for the third time", completing the count begun in verse 16 ("a second time").

decisions.choice: A third time he asked him (B); For the third time Jesus asked him (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16: the present "says" becomes "asked" at Balanced and Readable because it introduces a question (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15). "Love" stays the same word as in verses 15 and 16 (rendering decision r-en-2 at 21:15).

source.text: ἐλυπήθη ὁ Πέτρος ὅτι εἶπεν αὐτῷ τὸ τρίτον· Φιλεῖς με;

records.literal_gloss: Was grieved the Peter because he said to him the third [time], "Do you love me?"

en.L: Peter was grieved because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to him the third [time], "Do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.B: Peter was hurt because Jesus asked him a third time, "Do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"
en.R: Peter felt very sad because Jesus asked him a third time, "Do you love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

decisions.choice: Peter was grieved because he was asked a third time
decisions.reason: John gives the reason plainly: it was the third asking that hurt Peter. The verb (λυπέω) means to feel pain or sorrow, not to be offended.

decisions.choice: three questions recall Peter's three denials
decisions.reason: Peter had denied Jesus three times by a charcoal fire, as Jesus had foretold (13:38; 18:17, 25-27). Now, by another charcoal fire (21:9), Jesus asks him three times whether he loves him, and three times gives him the care of his flock. The third question would remind Peter of his third denial; it also lets him say three times what he had three times denied.

decisions.choice: the grief is at the third asking; whether the change of verb added to it is uncertain
alternatives: Peter was grieved because Jesus now used the other verb for love, as if doubting even the love Peter had claimed
decisions.reason: John repeats the question exactly as Jesus asked it the third time, with Peter's own verb. Those who see a distinction between the verbs take this as part of the hurt. But the sentence names "the third time" as the cause, not the choice of word (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: was hurt (B); felt very sad (R); Jesus asked (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Grieved" is formal in modern English. "Hurt" carries the pain of the Greek word without suggesting that Peter was offended; Readable uses the plainest words. Balanced and Readable name Jesus and say "asked", since "said" here introduces a question.

source.text: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Κύριε, πάντα σὺ οἶδας, σὺ γινώσκεις ὅτι φιλῶ σε.

records.literal_gloss: And he said to him, "Lord, all things you know, you know that I love you."

en.L: And he said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, all things {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.B: Peter replied, "Lord, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know everything; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."
en.R: Peter said, "Lord, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know everything. You know that I love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}."

decisions.choice: you know all things: Peter confesses what the disciples had said in 16:30
decisions.reason: On the night before the cross the disciples said, "Now we know that you know all things" (16:30). John has shown again and again that Jesus knows what is in people (1:47-48; 2:24-25; 6:64; 13:11). Peter now stakes everything on that knowledge, not on his own record.

decisions.choice: the two verbs for "know" (οἶδας and γινώσκεις) mean the same here
alternatives: you know all things in general; you recognize, by experience, that I love you
decisions.reason: Peter uses two different verbs for "know" in one breath. John uses both of Jesus's knowledge (2:24-25; 13:3, 7), and this passage varies its words throughout (see the decision on verse 17, last sentence). The second verb can be taken as knowledge gained by seeing and experiencing, but nothing in the sentence requires it.

decisions.choice: I love you: Peter's answer is the same in substance as before
decisions.reason: Peter uses the same verb for love as in his first two answers (meaning decision m1 at 21:15).

decisions.choice: know ... know, at every level
decisions.reason: The same English verb for both, because they mean the same here (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable drop the opening "And" and use normal English order; they name Peter, Balanced with "replied" since he is answering; Readable starts a new sentence at the second "You know".

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Βόσκε τὰ πρόβατά μου.

records.literal_gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "Feed the sheep of me.

decisions.choice: feed / shepherd and lambs / sheep: one charge in varied words
alternatives: three distinct tasks or three different groups (young believers, mature believers, and so on)
decisions.reason: Across verses 15-17 John varies almost every word: two verbs for love (verse 15), two for "know" (verse 17), "feed" (βόσκω) and "shepherd" (ποιμαίνω), "lambs" (ἀρνίον) and "sheep" (πρόβατον). Each pair is close in meaning, and the passage gives no sign that the variations mark separate groups or tasks. Together they give one charge: care for those who belong to Jesus, as he cares for them (10:11-16).

decisions.choice: sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: little sheep: a diminutive form (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: As in verse 16 (meaning decision m2 there), some manuscripts read the diminutive "little sheep"; the sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Jesus's words run on into verse 18
decisions.reason: The charge to feed the sheep leads straight into Jesus's word about how Peter will end his life (verses 18-19); the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11), and so will Peter.

decisions.choice: Feed, as in verse 15
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 15 gets the same English, so that "Feed" in verses 15 and 17 frames "Shepherd" in verse 16 as in the Greek. The quotation stays open because Jesus goes on speaking in verse 18.

source.text: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι, ὅτε ἦς νεώτερος, ἐζώννυες σεαυτὸν καὶ περιεπάτεις ὅπου ἤθελες· ὅταν δὲ γηράσῃς, ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σου, καὶ ἄλλος σε ζώσει καὶ οἴσει ὅπου οὐ θέλεις.

records.literal_gloss: Amen, amen I say to you, when you were younger, you were girding yourself and were walking about where you were wanting; but when you grow old, you will stretch out the hands of you, and another you will gird and will carry where not you want.

en.L: Truly, truly I say to you, when you were younger, you used to put a belt on yourself and walk where you wanted; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will put a belt on you and carry [you] where you do not want [to go]."
en.B: Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were younger you fastened your own belt and went wherever you wished. But when you have grown old, you will stretch out your hands, and then someone else will fasten a belt on you and take you where you do not wish to go."
en.R: I tell you the truth: when you were younger, you put on your own belt and went anywhere you wanted to go. But when you are an old man, you will stretch out your hands. Someone else will tie a belt around you and take you where you do not want to go."

decisions.choice: put on a belt: tie the long outer clothes up with a belt, ready to walk or work; done by another, it may also hint at being bound
alternatives: be tied up with ropes, as a prisoner
decisions.reason: People wore long, loose robes and fastened a belt round them before setting out or starting work (compare 13:4; Luke 12:35). A young man does this for himself and goes where he likes. When another does it for him, he is no longer free: the words fit a helpless old man being dressed, and they also fit a prisoner being bound and led away to die, which is how verse 19 explains them.

decisions.choice: stretch out your hands: most likely a veiled pointer to death by crucifixion
alternatives: the gesture of a helpless old man reaching out for someone to dress him and lead him
decisions.reason: Verse 19 says Jesus was showing by what kind of death Peter would glorify God, the phrase John used of Jesus's own crucifixion (12:33; 18:32). Greek and Roman writers sometimes spoke of the hands being stretched out of a person put on a cross, and Christian writers from about AD 200 onward say that Peter was crucified in Rome. Against this, the stretching out of the hands comes before the belt and the leading away, not after them. The words are a veiled saying, and the decision is marked uncertain.

decisions.choice: younger: when you were young, compared with now
decisions.reason: The word is the comparative of "young", contrasting Peter's earlier years with the old age to come (γηράσῃς, "you grow old"). It does not mean Peter is old now.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: put a belt on / fasten a belt / tie a belt (for the verb of girding); carry (L), take (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Gird" is no longer everyday English. Saying "belt" keeps the picture of the Greek, which allows both dressing and binding (meaning decision m1), rather than choosing one. The verb for "carry" is also used of leading or bringing someone; Balanced and Readable say "take". Literal supplies "you" and "to go", which the Greek leaves understood.

source.text: τοῦτο δὲ εἶπεν σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ δοξάσει τὸν θεόν.

records.literal_gloss: This now he said signifying by what kind of death he will glorify the God.

en.L: Now this {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God.
en.B: He said this to show by what kind of death Peter would glorify God.
en.R: Jesus said this to show the kind of death by which Peter would bring glory to God.

decisions.choice: the narrator explains Jesus's words, with the phrase used of Jesus's own death
decisions.reason: John steps out of the scene to tell the reader what Jesus meant, in nearly the same words he used of Jesus's death ("signifying by what kind of death he was about to die", 12:33; 18:32). Peter will die as his Lord died. "Signifying" means pointing to something by a hint rather than saying it outright.

decisions.choice: Peter's death will glorify God
decisions.reason: In John the cross is where the Son glorifies the Father (12:23-28; 13:31-32; 17:1, 4). Peter's death, faithful to the end, will also bring glory to God.

decisions.choice: Peter (B, R); Jesus said ... bring glory to God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Peter, so that the second "he" is not taken as Jesus. Balanced keeps the wording of 12:33 ("He said this to show ..."). Readable names Jesus and says "bring glory to" for "glorify". It does not add "on a cross" as 12:33 does, because here the kind of death is less certain (meaning decision m2 at verse 18).

source.text: καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν λέγει αὐτῷ· Ἀκολούθει μοι.

records.literal_gloss: And this having said, he says to him, "Follow me."

en.L: And having said this, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Follow me: the call to discipleship, now including following Jesus in death
decisions.reason: Jesus called his first disciples with these words (1:43). On the last night he told Peter, "You cannot follow me now ... but later you will follow" (13:36), and he had said that whoever serves him must follow him, and where he is, his servant will be (12:24-26). Now, after foretelling Peter's death, Jesus renews the call: Peter will follow him in life and, in the end, in the way he dies.

decisions.choice: Follow: keep on following
decisions.reason: The command is in the present tense, which in Greek points to a continuing way of life, not a single step.

decisions.choice: told him (B); Then Jesus said to Peter (R)
decisions.reason: The present "says" becomes a past tense (rendering decision r-en-1 at 21:15). Readable names both persons and puts "After saying this" as "Then". Every level keeps the short "Follow me" of 1:43 and 13:36.
